**On What We Cannot Know at the End**

Not every man knows what he will sing or feel as he watches life sail away toward its end. We imagine, perhaps, that we have prepared ourselves—that we have rehearsed our final thoughts and settled our final accounts. Yet the truth is that no one can predict the shape of his own heart in that last hour. The song we believe we will sing may dissolve into silence, or into something entirely unforeseen. The feelings we expect to hold may give way to emotions we have never before encountered.

A person cannot know what he will hope for once it becomes clear that he can never return to the past. So long as we believe the door behind us remains open, our hopes are ordinary and familiar. But when that door closes for good—when the possibility of return is finally extinguished—the human spirit reaches for something new. What that something is, we cannot say in advance. Hope does not vanish when the past becomes irretrievable; it merely transforms into a form we cannot recognize until we arrive there.

When ordinary pleasures like pruning roses or watching sunsets vanish, no one knows what he will find in their place. These small comforts anchor us to the world, giving our days their gentle rhythm. Yet when they slip away, as one day they must, the emptiness they leave is not necessarily emptiness at all. Perhaps something else rushes in to fill it—some quieter, deeper awareness that we could never have imagined while our hands were still busy among the thorns and our eyes still fixed upon the dying light.

Eventually, the weight of the past leans against nothing. All the years we have accumulated, all the memories we have carried, come to rest against an absence. The stories of the natural world—the turning of seasons, the blooming and withering of every living thing—reach their inevitable conclusion. Nature completes its long narrative, and we are folded quietly back into its silence.

And so we return to where we began: not every man knows what awaits him, or what he will sing, as death slips his ship into final darkness. The voyage ends as mysteriously as it was undertaken. Whatever songs we carry, whatever hopes we hold, whatever we discover in the vanishing of familiar things—these remain unknown to us until the very moment they are upon us. This is the last and deepest uncertainty of being human: that we cannot know ourselves fully until we are already passing beyond knowing.

# Meditation on Mortality: An Analysis of Mark Strand's Poem

Mark Strand's poem offers a profound meditation on mortality and the fundamental uncertainty that surrounds death. Rather than approaching this weighty subject through direct declaration, Strand employs an extended metaphor of a departing ship—an image that has long served literature as a symbol for the soul's journey away from the shores of the living. Through this poetic device, he transforms the abstract concept of dying into something tangible and visual, allowing readers to witness the slow, inevitable drift toward an unknown horizon.

At the heart of the poem lies a poignant awareness of what death takes from us: not grand possessions or worldly achievements, but rather life's simple pleasures. It is in these small, everyday experiences—the ordinary moments that constitute the texture of daily existence—that Strand locates the true value of being alive. Their loss becomes the measure of what death represents, making mortality not an intellectual abstraction but an intimate, personal deprivation that every reader can feel.

The poem's power derives significantly from its repeated refrain, the haunting phrase that "not every man knows." This recurring line functions as both structural anchor and thematic pulse, returning again and again to remind us of the essential mystery at the core of human existence. What lies beyond death remains genuinely unknowable—no certainty, no revelation, no map of the territory that awaits us. This refrain captures a truth that is at once humbling and universal: regardless of our knowledge, our faith, or our preparations, we all approach the final threshold in ignorance of what waits on the other side.

In weaving together these elements, Strand illuminates the shared human condition of facing death without the comfort of knowledge. The poem holds two truths in delicate balance: the inevitability of our final passage and the profound mystery that shrouds it. Death will come to all—this much is certain—yet what it means, where it leads, and what becomes of us remains forever beyond our grasp. Through his careful imagery and insistent refrain, Strand does not offer answers or false consolation. Instead, he invites us to contemplate our mortality honestly, acknowledging both the fear and the wonder inherent in confronting the great unknown that concludes every human life.

# When No One Is Watching

There is an old saying that character is revealed not by what we do in public, but by how we behave **when** no one is **watching**. It is a simple idea, yet it carries surprising weight in our daily lives.

Think about the small choices we make throughout the day. Do you return the extra change a cashier accidentally hands you? Do you follow the rules of the road even on an empty street at midnight? These moments are **not** witnessed by anyone, and yet they shape the person you truly are.

## The Value of Unseen Actions

The most honest version of ourselves appears in private. **When** we are being observed, it is natural to perform, to present our best face to the world. But integrity is what remains **when** the audience disappears. It is doing the right thing not for applause, not for reward, but simply because it is right.

Consider the employee who works just as diligently **when** the boss steps away. Consider the friend who keeps a secret even **when** revealing it would bring attention. These people understand that virtue is not a performance.

## Building Genuine Character

You cannot fake authenticity forever. The habits we practice in solitude eventually become who we are in public. If we are careless **when** no one is **watching**, that carelessness will eventually surface. But if we hold ourselves to a high standard even in private, that discipline becomes second nature.

So the next time you find yourself alone, facing a small decision that seems to matter to no one, remember: it matters to **you**. The choices you make when **not** being watched are the truest reflection of your character.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the style of Mark Strand about mortality and what a man faces at the end of life.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Last Inventory**

There is a room a man comes to
at the end, where the furniture
has been carried out
and the walls give back
nothing but his breathing.

He stands at the window
of a house that is no longer his
and watches the light
fold itself away
like a letter he never finished.

What he owned is elsewhere now.
The names of things
loosen from the things themselves
and drift off, weightless,
into the going dark.

He thinks: I was here.
He thinks: the field remembers nothing,
the road forgets my walking,
and the sea that once held my reflection
has smoothed it out of being.

There is no ceremony.
Only the slow undressing,
the giving back of hands, of hours,
of the small light he carried
without knowing he carried it.

And when the door opens
onto whatever is not a room,
he steps through the way a word
steps out of a mouth
and is not heard again—

leaving the chair,
leaving the window and its emptied hour,
leaving the shape of himself
in the air behind him,
already closing over.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a free-verse poem that meditates on death using the extended metaphor of a ship sailing away into darkness.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Leaving**

There is a harbor where the light
grows thin, where water forgets
the shape of shore.

I watched you loosen from the dock—
not suddenly, but the way rope
lets go of its own memory,
fiber by patient fiber.

The sails took wind I could not feel.
They swelled with something
on the far side of the air,
some breath the living
are not built to give.

I stood at the edge of the wooden world
and called across the widening dark,
but the sea between us
was already writing its long sentence,
each wave a word
that would not come back.

You did not wave.
Perhaps you could not.
Perhaps the hands that steer a leaving vessel
must stay closed around the wheel,
holding a course
no chart of ours has drawn.

Smaller now. A lantern.
Then the idea of a lantern.
Then the place where a lantern used to be—
that stubborn ghost of glow
the eye insists on
long after the wick is gone.

And here is the cruelty I did not expect:
the horizon does not open.
It closes like a mouth,
swallowing the last mast whole,
and the night stitches itself shut
over the seam where you slipped through.

I tell myself you are still sailing.
That somewhere past the curve
where our seeing fails,
the water keeps its promise to the keel,
and you go on—
carried, not drowned,
gathered by a distance
that has no other shore
I am permitted yet to name.

I turn back toward the small lit houses.
The harbor holds its empty berth
like a wound it will not close,
and I learn the oldest arithmetic:
that love is what remains
standing on the dock,
still leaning toward the dark,
still certain that departure
is only another word
for somewhere we have not yet learned
to follow.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a melancholic poem beginning with "Not every man knows what he shall sing at the end."
counterfactuals.output:
**Not Every Man Knows What He Shall Sing at the End**

Not every man knows what he shall sing at the end,
when the light thins to a rumor at the sill
and the house grows quiet as an unposted letter.
Some carry a tune they meant to learn
and never did—it waited in them like a coat
left hanging in a room no longer entered.

I have heard the old ones hum against the dark,
half-remembered psalms, a mother's name,
the syllables of towns dissolved to fields.
What rises is not always what we saved.
The heart is a poor curator of its treasures;
it keeps the accidental, loses the adored.

Perhaps that is the mercy and the wound:
we do not choose the last note we let go.
It chooses us, the way a season turns—
not asked, not answered, simply come.
And whether it is grief or gratitude
that shapes the throat, no living man can say.

So let me practice now, while breath is cheap,
some small, unhurried gladness for the world:
the smell of rain arriving on the stone,
the way a friend once laughed and meant it wholly.
If I must sing an ending unrehearsed,
let it at least be humble, and my own.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a lyrical poem about aging and uncertainty, using imagery of sunsets, moonlight, clouds, and birds in flight.
counterfactuals.output:
# Passage of Light

The sun descends in amber grace,
Each evening slower than the last,
And in the sky's unhurried face
I read the letters of my past.

Once I flew with morning birds,
Their wings a promise, sharp and bright—
Now I watch them, wordless, blurred,
Dissolve into the coming night.

The clouds drift on, uncertain, gray,
They gather, part, and gather still,
Like all the things I meant to say,
Like all the plans I never will.

What is this dusk that finds me here,
Half-golden and half-turned to shade?
I cannot name the thing I fear,
Nor hold the light before it fades.

Yet moonlight comes, a gentler friend,
To silver what the day made plain,
And though I cannot know the end,
The soft night does not ask my name.

So let me be a cloud tonight,
Unmoored, unhurried, drifting slow—
A bird still lifting into flight
Toward somewhere I may never know.

The sun will set. The moon will rise.
The birds will trace their fading arc.
And I will meet these questioned skies
With open hands, into the dark.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a contemplative poem about facing the unknown of death, repeating the phrase "not every man knows" and ending with a ship slipping into darkness.
counterfactuals.output:
**Not Every Man Knows**

Not every man knows the hour of his leaving,
the way the light will thin against the wall,
how the ordinary morning of his breathing
becomes the last, or if he'll know at all.

Not every man knows what waits beyond the doorway—
whether a country, or a quiet field,
whether the dead are gathered there, or no way
exists to say what silence keeps concealed.

Not every man knows how to loose his grip
on all the small and shining things he made,
the names, the hands, the warm familiar ship
of self he steered through every light and shade.

Not every man knows peace when it is offered,
nor fear its weight when courage falls away;
we take the coin the ferryman has proffered
and cannot read the writing, come what may.

Not every man knows—yet every man must go
where knowing ends and only going stays,
out past the harbor's last remembered glow,
past all the reckoning of nights and days.

And so he sets his sail without a chart,
no lantern but the beating of his heart,
and watches, as the shoreline shrinks and parts,
his ship slip quiet into the dark.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
